# WITTGENSTEIN AND THE BACKGROUND

John R. Searle

## I. THE PHILOSOPHICAL PROJECT

For the past fifty or so years I have been engaged in a single philosophical project, and specific topics on which I worked, such as speech acts, consciousness, intentionality, rationality, and social ontology, are all aspects of that larger project. I did philosophy professionally for a couple of decades before I fully realized the nature of the overall project and how all the various parts fitted in. As a preliminary formulation we might say that the project is to give an account of the human reality—the reality of such phenomena as language, consciousness, intentionality, free will, rationality, aesthetic experiences, ethics, and society—in a way that is both consistent with, and a natural development from, the basic facts of the universe as described by physics, chemistry, and for our little corner of the universe, evolutionary biology. How, in a world that consists entirely of mindless, meaningless physical particles in fields of force, can there be speech acts, consciousness, intentionality, rationality, free will, ethics, and aesthetics, as well as the human social reality of money, property, government, marriage, and philosophy conferences? I regard this as the central overriding question in contemporary philosophy, and indeed in contemporary intellectual life. My investigations deal with many traditional philosophical

questions, such as those concerning mind and meaning, as well as some that have not been part of mainstream analytic philosophy, such as those concerning social ontology.

questions, such as those concerning mind and meaning, as well as some that have not been part of mainstream analytic philosophy, such as those concerning social ontology.

A distinctive feature of my approach is that it is resolutely naturalistic while insisting on the reality of the phenomena being investigated. The accounts that I give are fully naturalistic in the sense that all of the human phenomena are regarded as parts of nature. We live in one world, not two or three or twenty-seven, and all parts of that world, from protons to presidents and from electrons to elections, have to fit together. By "fit together" I mean not just that the accounts of the different types of phenomena must be consistent with each other, but that the higher-level phenomena of consciousness, intentionality, and social ontology must be explained as natural forms that the lower-level phenomena take. If you understand electrons and elections right, you will see why some electrons have to participate in elections. No electrons, no elections. My sense of naturalism is emphatically different from what is common in analytic philosophy. Many philosophers who talk about "naturalizing consciousness" or "naturalizing intentionality" want to deny that consciousness and intentionality are irreducible mental phenomena. As Jerry Fodor says, "If aboutness is real, then it must really be something else." $^{1}$ I think that is exactly

wrong. Hunger and thirst are as real as digestion or photosynthesis, and all four—hunger, thirst, digestion, and photosynthesis—are real biological phenomena. So my account is naturalistic in an inclusive, rather than an exclusive, sense. The Boston Symphony Orchestra, Proust's recollections, and the British Wittgenstein Society are as much a part of nature as Niagara Falls or the trees that grow in Hertfordshire.

On the account I propose, language is an extension of pre-linguistic intentional phenomena such as beliefs and desires. We use pre-linguistic forms of intentionality to create linguistic meanings. And with the creation of speaker meanings as extensions of biologically more basic forms of intentionality, the evolution of conventions for expressing speaker meaning is a natural development. Once human creatures have a language, the creation of a social reality of families, private property, and political power is a natural extension of language, because all of these are created by and partly constituted by a certain type of speech act that I call a "Status Function Declaration." $^{2}$

I have been influenced by Wittgenstein in ways that I will explain in a moment, but I take it that the whole enterprise is profoundly counter to Wittgenstein's conception of philosophy. There is nothing therapeutic about it. It is an attempt to build comprehensive systematic theories of various human domains such as mind, language, society, and rationality.

About certain of my results I feel reasonably confident. I feel reasonably good about my theories of consciousness and intentionality as I have expounded them in a number of books and articles. And I think my theory of meaning and speech acts is on the right track. I also feel optimistic about my account of Social Ontology as outlined in the Construction of Social Reality and extended in my most recent book, Making the Social World.

Several other parts of my account are in various ways inadequate. My account of free will is unable to answer the questions that prompted the investigation in the first place. And I have no theory of aesthetics, or at least nothing worth calling a theory.

## II. THE THESIS OF THE BACKGROUND.

Several other parts of my account are in various ways inadequate. My account of free will is unable to answer the questions that prompted the investigation in the first place. And I have no theory of aesthetics, or at least nothing worth calling a theory.

## II. THE THESIS OF THE BACKGROUND.

One subject on which I have published fairly extensively, but on which I still regard my views as unsatisfactory, is what I call the Background. Here my views are explicitly influenced by Wittgenstein, not in the sense that I think my views are the same as his, but in the sense that my views have been in part provoked by my reading and reflections on his later work.

What exactly is the thesis of the Background? In its simplest form it is the claim that linguistic meaning in particular and all intentionality in general only function given a Background of abilities, capacities, tendencies, dispositions, and other causal structures that do not themselves consist of meanings or other intentional phenomena. In order to work with such things as sentences, beliefs, and desires, you have to have a set of abilities that do not themselves consist entirely in more sentences, beliefs, and desires. To understand this claim it is helpful to see the arguments for it, at least the arguments that initially convinced me. Let us start with sentences. An examination of the use of sentences to perform speech acts reveals that the literal semantic content, the literal meaning of the sentence by itself, is not sufficient to determine truth conditions or other conditions of satisfaction. What more is required? Well consider this sentence: "I am attending a Wittgenstein conference in Hertfordshire, England." Ask yourself what else I would have to know, or at least believe, in order to use that sentence to perform the speech act of stating that I am attending a Wittgenstein conference in Hertfordshire, England, and thereby expressing the corresponding belief.

It turns out that I have to believe a large number of other things in order to understand the sentence in the way that I do and for the speech act to have the kind of sense to me that it has. In my case I have to believe that Hertfordshire is located in the United Kingdom and that England is part of the United Kingdom. I have to believe that conferences are gatherings attended by groups of people, usually sharing some common interests. At these gatherings, a lot of talking goes on, and sometimes individual speakers get up and make speeches, as I did. I have to believe that Wittgenstein was an influential philosopher, a philosopher who produced books that I am familiar with, and so on. I call this network of beliefs, etc., which enable us to make sense of any particular sentence, speech act, or belief, the Network. But it turns out that the Network, at least as I have described it, is not enough to account for the functioning of sentences, speech acts, and intentional states. There are various ways to see this. One is that if you follow out the various threads of the Network, you eventually get to things that do not seem like beliefs, or at least not like the beliefs that I have been articulating. Is it one of my beliefs that conferences are generally held at or near the surface of the earth, rather than, say, on Mars, or by people floating freely in outer space? That during the course of the conference gravitational attraction continues to function? That at least some of the people at conferences are sometimes conscious? If I believe the negation of any of these, I would have to have a different conception of a conference, but it seems odd to think of these as just more beliefs. I want to argue that the whole Network of our beliefs (as well as desires, fears, hopes, etc.) only functions given a Background of things I take for granted, and many of these things I take for granted are in the form of practices, dispositions, ways of behaving, and general know-how. This point, I think, will be even clearer if you think what sorts of abilities I

must have in order to form and carry out the intention to attend such a conference. Without going into details it seems to me that I have to have a set of skills and dispositions and capacities generally. I have to be able to cope with moving my body through space and time, getting on and off buses and trains, moving other objects, and dealing with people. There are a lot of intentional states involved in these activities. So, for example, I have to believe a particular train is the right train to get on. But the totality of intentional states is not sufficient to determine appropriate behavior. In addition, you need the Background of abilities.

One might be tempted to think that the example I have chosen, "I am now attending a Wittgenstein conference in Hertfordshire England," is too context dependent to serve as a model for the interpretation of all semantic content; that if one took, for example, statements in arithmetic one would find that no Background or Network is essential for their understanding. I think this is wrong, and I think Wittgenstein gives some good arguments to show this. We think that 3+4 equals 7 in a way that is absolutely timeless and context free. But suppose there were a tribe that insisted on doing arithmetic with actual sets. Generally you will have different sorts of cases. In one case A = 3, B = 4 and A +B=7. But in another case A = 3, B = 4, and A +B=5.

And it is no good in dealing with this example to appeal to the cardinality of set union. Because, of course, how we count the cardinality of the set union is also a matter of

the practices in which we are trained. In this way of counting, the cardinality of set union for Case 2 is 7.

So initially, the thesis of the Background is that in order to fix the conditions of satisfaction of any sentence, speech act, or intentional state, you require more than just the content of the sentence, speech act, or intentional state, and you need more than a Network of other such contents. Such intentional entities are not self interpreting and you have to have a set of abilities in order to interpret them or in order to apply them. I certainly have not demonstrated the thesis of the Background, but I am suggesting that if you look at examples of semantic contents that are everywhere around you—for example, by looking at a daily newspaper or listening to a conversation you might be able to convince yourself, as I became convinced, that semantic content as traditionally construed is, by itself, insufficient to determine interpretation.

I tried also to do a sort of minimal taxonomy of the Background and my efforts here are somewhat reminiscent of Danièle Moyal-Sharrock's discussion of what she calls "hinge statements" in Wittgenstein. $^{3}$ So I make a distinction between what I call the Deep Background, which is common to all human beings, and Local Cultural Practices. This corresponds roughly to Moyal-Sharrock's distinction between universal hinges and local hinges. Examples of universal hinges would be that human beings move about on the surface of the earth, that they are located in space and time, that they walk upright and eat through their mouths. Ex-

amples of local cultural practices would be such things as what constitutes appropriate behavior for men and women respectively, how far apart people stand from each other in a conversation, and what sort of posture it is appropriate to adopt in particular situations.

amples of local cultural practices would be such things as what constitutes appropriate behavior for men and women respectively, how far apart people stand from each other in a conversation, and what sort of posture it is appropriate to adopt in particular situations.

My notion of local cultural practices also has some affinities with Bourdieu's concept of the habitus. $^{4}$ Cutting across the deep and local distinction is a distinction between how things are and how to do things, and roughly speaking, this distinction corresponds to the traditional distinction between the theoretical and practical. How things are has to do with such things as the solidity of objects and the constancy of gravitational force. How to do things has to do with such things as how to walk or how to cut with a knife. Again, there is no sharp distinction, because one can cut with a knife made of steel but not with a knife made of butter, and thus how to do things depends on how things are.

## III. SOME PROBLEMS WITH THE THESIS: THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN BACKGROUND AND NETWORK.

So far I have just sketched the thesis of the Background. Imagine that I have filled in all the details and have given you a more thoroughgoing account of the operation of the Background. All the same, I am not satisfied with it. Why not? Apart from the fact that the account is rather vague and loose, it rests on a distinction between the Network as a set of "representations" such as beliefs and desires and the Background as a set of "abilities." But on my own terms the distinction cannot be made in quite that form, because on my own account, an intentional state such as a belief or desire, when it is completely unconscious, exists as a dispositional capacity of the brain to produce the state in the conscious form. Even when I am sound asleep, I believe that George Washington was the first president of the United States. What fact about me makes it the case that I have that belief? It can only

be that my brain has the capacity, other things equal, to produce that belief in the conscious form. That is one objection to the distinction. The unconscious Network consists in Background abilities. Another objection, which I will explain in more detail when we get into Wittgenstein, is that there appears to be a kind of match between Background presuppositions and beliefs. Moyal-Sharrock, in her book Understanding Wittgenstein On Certainty (2007), comments on this when she treats what I think of as Background phenomena as "nonpropositional beliefs." Later I will have something to say about her treatment of the issue.

## IV. WITTGENSTEIN AND THE UNGROUNDED

On the account I have presented, the thesis of the Background is a thesis about the operation of intentionality, including language. It is a thesis about the conditions of possibility of the functioning of perception, action, thinking, speaking, and any other form of mental phenomena involving intentionality. It has implications for epistemology, but there is nothing specifically epistemic about it. Many of Wittgenstein's most important remarks about these issues are in a book that is specifically about epistemic issues, On Certainty. I now want to say some things about Wittgenstein's conceptions.

Wittgenstein emphasizes that there are ungrounded ways of acting, ways of doing things. These are examples of what I mean by the Background. The temptation is to think that he is making a traditional pragmatist-style plea for the priority of "practical reason" over "theoretical reason." But I think that is a mistaken interpretation. For the purposes of this discussion, thinking and talking are also ways of acting. His point is that the ground of our doing something is not something that in every case has to be hypothesized and established in order for us to do it. Think of children playing a game of football. This

requires a field and a ball, but unless the external world exists, there is no field and no ball. But it does not follow that the children must first prove the existence of, or at least have faith in the existence of, the external world before they can play football. Rather, as Wittgenstein says, they just act. What does that mean, "They just act"? I now want to explore some of these issues.

Consider a striking quotation from Wittgenstein:

Consider a striking quotation from Wittgenstein:

The squirrel does not infer by induction that it is going to need stores next winter as well. And no more do we need a law of induction to justify our actions or our predictions. (On Certainty, sec. 287)

In my terminology I would put this point by saying that the practice of proceeding by induction is a Background ability we have. It is not something that requires justification but is rather the standard by which we justify other things. I think Wittgenstein's claim is correct, but to someone brought up on traditional philosophy, it will seem puzzling. Surely, if the squirrel could think and came to doubt the validity of induction, it might come to seem that his storing nuts for the winter was not rationally justified, but instead a leap in the dark, an act of faith without any rational justification. What is wrong with such a philosophical squirrel? I am suggesting, though I have not yet argued for it, that the practice of induction is simply a Background disposition or ability, and it is typical of a certain class of Background dispositions that if you try to treat them as hypotheses, this immediately creates insurmountable philosophical problems, because as hypotheses they seem unjustified.

## V. EXTERNAL REALISM AND THE BACKGROUND

Consider another example. Kant thought it was a scandal that no one had yet proven the existence of the external world. Now why do

we not all get busy and do it? Well, Moore indeed, thought he had. He argued, "I know that these hands exist. If these hands exist then the external world exists. So the external world exists." $^{5}$

Let us call the thesis that the external world exists "external realism." I think there was something wrong with Kant's demand for a proof of external realism and that Moore's attempted proof simply misses the point. But on the surface, at least, they both look right. Kant sees correctly that unless external realism is true, a rather large percentage of our beliefs and hypotheses, etc., cannot be true. Because so much depends on the truth of external realism, we had better get busy and prove it. Moore's proof is a standard form of proof which in other contexts we regard as perfectly acceptable. If one wants to know whether or not a certain sort of thing exists, for example, albino penguins, then a standard form of proof would be to produce examples of them. Here are two albino penguins, therefore albino penguins exist. Do external objects exist? Here are two external objects, says Moore, my two hands. Therefore, external objects exist.

Against both Kant and Moore, one can present a traditional type of philosophical argument to the effect that presupposition of external realism is a condition of intelligibility of a very large number of our representations, speech acts, theories, beliefs, etc. If you want to know whether or not dinosaurs existed in the Pleistocene, or whether the Ford Motor Company ever made a car with a 12-cylinder engine, or whether George Washington had false teeth, in every case it seems you have to presuppose the existence of a reality independent of your representations. Similarly, if you want to go skiing, visit England, or even eat a good meal, it seems you can only do these if you believe that the real world exists. It is a mistake to think that this reality must consist of "material objects," but the Background presupposition is that there must be a way

things are independent of our representation of how they are. But if that is right, then what is wrong with the demand that one prove external realism, that one prove that there is a way that things are? The answer is that all forms of proof about the world, such as Moore's demonstration with his two hands presuppose external realism and consequently, external realism cannot be proved without circularity. But now why is that not grounds for skepticism? The same argument works for induction. The ability to reason from evidence to support general hypotheses presupposes the validity of induction, so induction cannot be proven, by gathering evidence, without circularity. But why is that not grounds for skepticism about induction?

The general point I want to make is this: for any activity there is a set of facts such that, unless those facts obtained, the activity could not exist. But then it looks as if anyone engaged in the activity must believe in the existence of those facts. You cannot, for example, play a game of football or vote in an election unless you believe football and elections exist. So it looks like you have to believe in the existence of such things in order to engage in the activity. But in a lot of philosophically puzzling cases, such as external realism, the validity of induction, the reality of the past, and the existence of other minds—it seems one is unable to justify a belief in the existence of the facts in question. And this in turn looks like it leads to some kind of skepticism. The main subject of this essay is to use the notion of the Background to overcome this difficulty.

## VI. THE RELATION OF BACKGROUND AND BELIEF

Many of the examples that Wittgenstein gives in On Certainty and that Moyal-Sharrock cites as local hinges would not be part of the Background in my sense. For example, the fact that Napoleon existed is, for me, a fact like any other. Of course, as Witt-

genstein keeps reminding us, not all of our beliefs are on the same footing, so my belief that Napoleon existed is much more solidly entrenched than my belief, for example, that his subordinate, Marechal Ney, was a great military commander. Neither belief is part of the Background. But when we get to the Deep Background, such features as external realism or our capacity for inductive reasoning, then I think there is a distinct overlap between my conception of the Background and the universal hinges. But Moyal-Sharrock cites all of these as cases of belief, or belief in at least one sense of belief. I am now going to try to sort out some of these issues.

Moyal-Sharrock claims that some beliefs are nonpropositional. This enables her to construe objective certainty as a kind of belief, and she gives three reasons for doing this. First, it enables us to ascribe belief to animals and nonlinguistic humans; second, it is the way we describe our own hinges when they are challenged; and third, we can think of belief as a continuum going from primitive nonpropositional attitudes to more sophisticated propositional attitudes (2007, p. 186). I have a totally different way of thinking of these matters.

1. The traditional terminology of "propositional attitudes" is confused. If I believe that it is raining, the surface structure of the sentence makes it look as if "believe" names a relation in which I stand to the proposition that it is raining. But that is a mistake generated by the surface structure of the sentence. The proposition is not the object of the belief or the assertion. It is rather, in each case, the content. Strictly speaking the belief is constituted by the proposition (construed as believed), and the assertion is constituted by the proposition (construed as asserted). A belief just is a believed proposition, and an assertion just is an asserted proposition. If I believe that Obama is president, then the object of

my belief is Obama, not the proposition. The proposition, to repeat, is the content of the belief, not its object. I cannot tell you what a disaster this muddled terminology has been for cognitive science, and maybe for philosophy, too.

my belief is Obama, not the proposition. The proposition, to repeat, is the content of the belief, not its object. I cannot tell you what a disaster this muddled terminology has been for cognitive science, and maybe for philosophy, too.

2. There is no such thing as a nonpropositional belief. All beliefs are beliefs that such and such is the case. This is because every belief has to set a condition, a truth condition, just as every desire has to set a satisfaction condition, and every intention has to set a carrying out condition. Conditions are by definition propositional because every condition is a condition that such and such. To put this point succinctly, there is a tight connection between belief, proposition conditions, and truth. Every belief sets a truth condition, and truth conditions are by definition propositional, because the truth condition is always a condition that such and such.

3. There is no need to postulate a continuum of senses of "belief" that goes from animals and nonlinguistic humans at one end to us inveterate talkers at the other. The sense in which my dog Gilbert believes someone is at the door and the sense in which I believe someone is at the door are exactly the same. In both cases there is a belief with propositional content, direction of fit, and conditions of satisfaction, in this case truth conditions. The linguists have a test for nonambiguity, namely, conjunction reduction, and that test works for these cases. I believe someone is at the door, and Gilbert believes someone is at the door. So both Gilbert and I believe that someone is at the door.

4. What about the relation of belief to the Background? For any activity there is a set of facts such that, unless those facts obtained, the activity could not exist. This makes it seem that for any activ-

ity, anyone engaged in the activity must believe in the existence of those facts. For example, I cannot vote in an election unless there is an election, so my voting requires a belief in the existence of the election. But similarly, it seems that the children cannot play a game of football unless external realism is true. No real world, no real game of football. So it looks as if the children must be metaphysicians after all. And what goes for the children goes for all of us. We must all believe in external realism. But for many philosophically puzzling phenomena, we do not know how to justify the belief in the relevant facts. How do we justify external realism, the existence of other minds, the reality of the past, the validity of induction, and a host of other favorite philosophical chestnuts?

## VII. WE JUST ACT

5. One of the consequences of the thesis of the Background is this: you can engage in an activity that could not exist unless certain facts existed without having a belief or other intentional state about those facts. How is this possible? Here we come to Wittgenstein's thesis of the primacy of acting, of practice. We just do it. We do not first have to prove the existence of the external world before we play football or hammer the nail into the board. We just play football or hammer. When the Background is functioning as Background, as skills, it does not function in the way of beliefs. I once tried to state this point as follows:

Realism, I want to say, is not a hypothesis belief, or philosophical thesis; realism is part of the Background in the following sense. My commitment to "realism" is exhibited by the fact that I live the way that I do: I drive my car, drink my beer, write my articles, give my lectures and ski my mountains. Now in addition

to all of these activities, each a manifestation of my intentionality, there isn't a further "hypothesis" that the real world exists. My commitment to the existence of the real world is manifested whenever I do pretty much anything. It is a mistake to treat that commitment as if it were a hypothesis, as if in addition to skiing, drinking, eating etc. I held a belief—there is a real world independent of my representations of it. $^{6}$

This passage was misunderstood by at least some of my critics. $^{7}$ The point I am making is that when an activity presupposes something, you do not always have to have a belief in the existence of that something in order to engage in the activity.

Yes, but all the same, could we form a belief? Could we state the universal hinges as beliefs in the way that Moyal-Sharrock does? And the answer is that we could, and indeed as philosophers we are typically tempted, to do so. But the point is that when the Background is functioning as Background, it does not function in the way that beliefs function. Well, how do beliefs function? I voted for Obama in the last presidential election because I believed that he would be a better president than McCain, and I thought I had good reasons for my belief. That is how beliefs function in our behavior. But when I eat lunch I do not in that way eat lunch because I believe the external world exists. I do not engage in my activities on the basis of beliefs in the existence of the facts that are presupposed by my activities. What then is the basis? Here again it seems to me Wittgenstein is right. The activity is in this sense "ungrounded." We just do it. We do not have to first establish the conditions of possibility.

Another way to put this point is to say that the belief derives from the activity and not conversely. We do not first have the belief and on that basis engage in the activity.Rather, we have the ability to do so,and we just engage in the activity. We can then form beliefs about the conditions under which it is possible to engage in the activity.

6. What then exactly is the relationship between beliefs and the Deep Background? Let us assume that I am right that there are no such things as nonpropositional beliefs. Let us suppose also that for any activity, there is a set of propositions such that if they were not true, the activity could not take place. Where Deep Background is concerned, we can always formulate those propositions as sets of "beliefs" that participants in the activity must have.

Against this picture I have been arguing, first, that the belief does not provide the ground for the activity. The activity is ungrounded. You can see this in the case of animals, and that was part of the point of the squirrel storing nuts for the winter. The squirrels do not store nuts because they think they have solved the problem of induction.

Second, you can always formulate a belief but the belief derives from the activity and not the activity from the belief. Again in the case of animals, the animals have the activity but they do not have the conceptual apparatus to formulate the belief.

Third, where certain traditional philosophical Background practices are concerned, to treat the presuppositions as hypotheses or beliefs inevitably leads to skepticism. How would we ever justify these beliefs?

7. This is not a "refutation of skepticism." It shows only that some of the power of skepticism derives from the fact that we assimilate the skeptical challenge to the wrong model. We treat the challenge as one of providing evidence for a hypothesis or belief. But in several of the cases where the skeptic is challenging us, we do not act on the basis of a hypothesis or a belief. Our actions are "ungrounded" not because they need a ground that we have somehow or other failed to provide, but because they do not need a ground. We can, and do, just act.

10. Another way to put this same point is this: if I believe the negation of certain propositions, I could not engage in the activities I do. But it does not follow from this that when I do engage in the activities, it is on the basis of my beliefs. So if I believed that people around me were unconscious automata, I could not respond to them as I do. But it does not follow from that fact that in order for me to respond to them as I do, I must hold the belief that they are all conscious. From the fact that if one disbelieves a proposition p one would no longer be able to engage in a certain form of normal behavior, it does not follow that when one engages the normal form of behavior, one thereby believes that p. So when I walk, if I truly disbelieve that the ground underneath me is solid, then it would alter my behavior, but it does not follow from this that I must form the belief that the ground underneath me is solid before I can walk. I can if I wish form the belief, but the belief derives from my capacity for the action and not conversely. You just act and then on the basis of your acting, or your capacity to act, you can then form an intentional state: I believe that such and such, but the ability to perform the action and the action are prior to the belief.

11. In a Wittgensteinian style, we might want to remind ourselves of the language game that we play with the word "believe." If I tell you, for example, that I believe it will rain tonight, you might ask me why I believe that, and I might answer by giving various considerations: clouds on the horizon, weather prediction on television, and falling barometer, for example. But for the Deep Background these sorts of considerations are not typically available. In the weather case I might in a pinch just say, "I have a hunch"

or even that it is just a "feeling" that it will rain. But it seems odd to say that I have a hunch that the real world exists, or at any rate that is how I feel that it exists. The idea of Deep Background as a matter of "belief" looks like a case of language going on holiday.

## VIII CONCLUSION

I said I was dissatisfied with my account of the Background, and I still am. But maybe we have made a little progress. As is often the case with Wittgenstein, he tries to get us to see the phenomena in a new light, from a different perspective.

The traditional view, which Wittgenstein was militating against in various forms, was that the mind consists of an inventory of mental states. These are all accessible to introspection. Furthermore, they are all on the same footing. The belief that the external world exists is just like the belief that I have two hands or that Obama is president. On this conception, mental processes are processes operating on the members of this inventory. Wittgenstein lived before the ascendance of the computational theory of mind, but I think he would have attacked it for the same sort of

reasons that he attacked the earlier inventory conception. On the computational conception there is still an inventory of mental states, but introspection drops out, and mental processes are thought of as computational processes operating on the formal structure of the members of the inventory.

Against this conception I have argued the states only work, they only function against a Background of capacities, tendencies, dispositions, etc., that cannot be accurately thought of as further states. Corresponding to these Background capacities we can always form beliefs. But we mistake the character the operation of the Background if we think it is based on beliefs. On the contrary, the operations are ungrounded. They are not based on anything in the way that traditional epistemologists thought of foundations. Of course, our practices are grounded in our biology and our culture, but these are not foundational in the Cartesian sense, because they do not give us justifications. The beliefs about the Background practices derive from the practices rather than forming a justification for the practices.
